question: After waiting until he was a hundred years old for his promised son, Abraham was tested when God told him to take that son and offer him as a burnt sacrifice on a specific mountain three days' journey away. Abraham rose early, saddled his donkey, took two servants and his son, and traveled in silence. The boy carried the wood for his own pyre up the slope. As Abraham raised the knife over his bound son on the altar, an angel called from heaven to stop him, and a ram caught by its horns in a thicket was sacrificed instead. What was the name of the mountain?
answer: Mount Moriah
choices: Mount Moriah
Mount Carmel
Mount Tabor
Mount Gilead
context: Genesis 22. Abraham named the place Yahweh-Yireh ('the Lord will provide'). Jewish tradition identifies Moriah with the rock under the later Temple Mount in Jerusalem. The boy on the wood asked his father where the lamb was; Abraham answered that God would provide it. The episode is called the Akedah ('binding') and is read each Rosh Hashanah.

question: Returning home after twenty years working for his uncle Laban, Jacob feared his estranged brother Esau — whom he had cheated of birthright and blessing. He sent his wives, sons, and flocks across the river Jabbok and stayed alone on the far bank that night. A mysterious man wrestled with him until dawn. Unable to overpower Jacob, the man touched the socket of Jacob's hip, dislocating it. Jacob refused to release him without a blessing, and the stranger renamed him Israel. Jacob renamed the place to mark where he had seen God face to face. What did he call it?
answer: Peniel — face of God
choices: Peniel — face of God
Bethel — house of God
Mizpah — watchtower
Gilgal — circle of stones
context: Genesis 32:22-32. Jacob limped from then on, and the Israelites traditionally do not eat the sciatic nerve from the hip-socket of animals in remembrance. The next morning Esau, far from attacking, ran to meet Jacob and embraced him. The name Israel means 'one who strives with God.'

question: Sold by his jealous brothers as a slave to Egypt, Joseph rose, fell, and was imprisoned on false charges from his master's wife. In prison he correctly interpreted dreams for Pharaoh's cupbearer and baker. Two years later Pharaoh himself dreamed of seven fat cows eaten by seven gaunt cows, and seven full ears of grain swallowed by seven withered ears. None of Egypt's wise men could interpret it. The cupbearer remembered Joseph. Pharaoh sent for him; Joseph said the two dreams meant the same thing. What did Joseph say the dreams predicted?
answer: Seven years of abundance followed by seven years of famine
choices: Seven years of abundance followed by seven years of famine
Seven plagues that would devastate every household in Egypt
Seven kings who would rise against Egypt from the east
Seven prophets who would condemn Pharaoh's court
context: Genesis 41. Pharaoh made Joseph second only to himself, putting him in charge of storing grain during the seven good years. When the famine came, Joseph's brothers — not recognizing him under Egyptian dress — came to Egypt to buy grain, and Joseph eventually revealed himself and brought his family to safety. Pharaoh gave him an Egyptian name, Zaphenath-Paneah.

question: Sold by his brothers into Egyptian slavery, Joseph was bought by Potiphar, captain of Pharaoh's guard, who recognized the boy's gifts and put him in charge of his entire household. Potiphar's wife began pressing Joseph daily to sleep with her. He refused, telling her he could not betray his master's trust or sin against God. One day she caught him alone, gripped his garment, and demanded he lie with her. Joseph fled the house, but she kept a piece of his clothing as evidence. What did she then claim to her husband and the household servants?
answer: That Joseph had tried to force himself on her and fled when she screamed
choices: That Joseph had tried to force himself on her and fled when she screamed
That Joseph had stolen jewelry from her dressing chamber
That Joseph had cursed Pharaoh and the gods of Egypt
That Joseph had plotted with foreign agents against her husband
context: Genesis 39. Potiphar had Joseph thrown into the king's prison. The keeper of the prison soon put Joseph in charge of all the other prisoners. Two of those prisoners would later be Pharaoh's cupbearer and baker, whose dreams Joseph interpreted — the chain of events that eventually led to his interpreting Pharaoh's own dreams.

question: Pharaoh, having let the Israelites leave Egypt after the ten plagues, changed his mind and sent his chariot army after them. The Israelites, trapped between the Red Sea and the advancing chariots, panicked and accused Moses of leading them out to die. A pillar of cloud moved between the two camps so that neither side could see the other through the night. Then Moses stretched out something over the sea, and a strong east wind drove the waters back all night, leaving dry ground between two walls of water. What did Moses stretch out over the sea?
answer: His staff
choices: His staff
His outer cloak
His sandals
The Tablets of the Law
context: Exodus 14. The Israelites crossed dry-shod. When the Egyptian chariots followed, Moses stretched the staff again and the waters returned, drowning Pharaoh's army. On the far shore Moses's sister Miriam led the women with tambourines in song: 'Sing to the Lord, for he has triumphed gloriously; horse and rider he has thrown into the sea.'

question: During the long wandering in the wilderness, the Israelites complained again against Moses and God, this time about the food. As punishment, venomous snakes appeared in the camp and bit many people, and some died. The people repented and begged Moses to pray for them. God told Moses to make an object and lift it up on a pole — anyone bitten who looked at it would live. What did Moses make and raise on the pole?
answer: A serpent cast in bronze
choices: A serpent cast in bronze
A wooden cross overlaid with gold
A silver dove with outstretched wings
A wooden staff topped with brass
context: Numbers 21:4-9. The bronze serpent was preserved as a sacred object until King Hezekiah destroyed it centuries later because the people had begun worshipping it as an idol, calling it Nehushtan. In the Gospel of John (3:14), Jesus invokes the image: 'As Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, so must the Son of Man be lifted up.'

question: Crossing the Jordan River into Canaan, Joshua's army faced the walled city of Jericho first. God gave Joshua unusual orders for siege. For six days the army was to march around the city in complete silence, with a specific group walking before the Ark of the Covenant carrying ram's-horn trumpets. On the seventh day they were to march around the city seven times, blow a long blast, and shout — and the walls would fall flat. Who walked before the Ark with the trumpets, and how many of them?
answer: Seven priests carrying seven ram's-horn trumpets
choices: Seven priests carrying seven ram's-horn trumpets
Twelve elders carrying twelve silver horns
Three captains carrying three bronze trumpets
Forty Levites carrying forty wooden flutes
context: Joshua 6. Only Rahab the prostitute and her family were spared — she had hidden Israelite spies earlier and had marked her window with a scarlet cord on the agreed signal. The number seven (priests, trumpets, days, circuits on the seventh day) saturates the story; archaeologists at Tell es-Sultan have debated for over a century how to read the collapsed walls.

question: The Canaanite general Sisera commanded nine hundred iron chariots and had oppressed Israel for twenty years. The prophet-judge Deborah, sitting beneath her palm tree, summoned the Israelite commander Barak and told him God would deliver Sisera into the hand of a woman. After a sudden storm bogged down his chariots, Sisera fled on foot and took refuge in the tent of a Kenite woman named Jael, who gave him milk and let him sleep. As he slept exhausted on the floor of her tent, Jael picked up a tent peg and a hammer and killed him. Where did she drive the peg?
answer: Through his temple, pinning his head to the ground
choices: Through his temple, pinning his head to the ground
Through his heart, leaving the peg buried in his chest
Through his throat, severing the windpipe at once
Through his thigh, leaving him to bleed slowly to death
context: Judges 4-5. The Song of Deborah (Judges 5) is one of the oldest passages in the Hebrew Bible — a victory ode in archaic Hebrew. It mocks Sisera's mother, who waits at her window wondering why the chariots are so long in returning. Deborah is the only woman in the Bible called a judge of Israel in her own right.

question: When the Midianites had ravaged Israel for seven years, an angel appeared to a farmer named Gideon hiding from raiders in a winepress, and told him he would deliver Israel. Gideon gathered an army of 32,000 men. God told him the army was too large — if they won, Israel would think they had saved themselves. Gideon sent home anyone who was afraid; 22,000 left. Still too many, God said. At a spring he watched the remaining men drink. He kept only the 300 who lapped water from cupped hands like a dog. What did the 300 carry in their attack?
answer: Trumpets, torches, and empty clay jars
choices: Trumpets, torches, and empty clay jars
Slings, smooth stones, and shepherds' staves
Bows, arrows, and bronze shields
Spears, oil lamps, and oxhide leather drums
context: Judges 7. Gideon split the 300 into three companies and surrounded the Midianite camp at night. At a signal they smashed the clay jars to reveal their hidden torches, blew the trumpets, and shouted 'A sword for the Lord and for Gideon!' The terrified Midianites turned on each other in the dark and fled, and Israel pursued them across the Jordan.

question: When Solomon became king of Israel after his father David's death, he went to the high place at Gibeon to offer a thousand burnt offerings. That night God appeared to him in a dream and said: Ask what I shall give you. Solomon was a young man, suddenly responsible for a great kingdom. He could have asked for long life, wealth, or the death of his enemies. Instead he asked for one specific thing, and God was so pleased by the request that he granted it AND added the things Solomon had not asked for. What did Solomon ask for?
answer: An understanding heart, to discern between good and evil
choices: An understanding heart, to discern between good and evil
Victory over every neighboring kingdom that threatened Israel
A son worthy to inherit the throne after his death
Permission to build a great temple in Jerusalem
context: 1 Kings 3:5-14. God answered: 'Because you have asked this, and have not asked for yourself long life or riches or the lives of your enemies, behold, I now do according to your word.' God added riches and honor as well. The first famous proof of Solomon's wisdom came shortly after, when two women came before him each claiming the same living baby.

question: The prophet Elijah, knowing his time on earth was ending, traveled from Gilgal to Bethel to Jericho to the Jordan, with his protege Elisha refusing to leave him at each stop. At the Jordan, Elijah rolled up his cloak, struck the water, and the river parted; they crossed on dry ground. On the far side Elijah asked: Tell me what I shall do for you before I am taken from you. Elisha asked a specific thing, which Elijah said was hard but possible if Elisha saw what would happen. Then a chariot and horses of fire separated them, and Elijah went up to heaven in a whirlwind. What had Elisha asked for?
answer: A double portion of Elijah's spirit
choices: A double portion of Elijah's spirit
Elijah's own cloak as a memorial of their years together
The gift of seeing all secrets hidden from other men
Long life equal to Elijah's own years in the wilderness
context: 2 Kings 2. Elisha did see the chariot of fire — and so received the double portion. He picked up Elijah's mantle, which had fallen as Elijah was taken up, struck the Jordan with it as Elijah had done, and the waters again parted. The watching prophets at Jericho recognized: 'The spirit of Elijah rests on Elisha.' Elijah's departure without dying is unique in the Hebrew Bible (Enoch is the only other figure said to be taken).

question: King Hezekiah of Judah lay dying of an infected boil. The prophet Isaiah came and told him to put his house in order — he would die. Hezekiah turned his face to the wall and wept bitterly, reminding God how faithfully he had served. Isaiah had not yet left the middle court when God told him to turn back: God would heal Hezekiah and add fifteen years to his life. Hezekiah asked for a sign. Isaiah offered him a choice — should the shadow on the palace sundial go forward ten steps or go back ten? Hezekiah chose what he thought was the harder miracle. Which did he choose?
answer: The shadow should go BACKWARD ten steps
choices: The shadow should go BACKWARD ten steps
The shadow should jump forward by twenty steps at noon
The sun itself should be hidden behind cloud for a full day
The moon should rise at midday over the temple roof
context: 2 Kings 20:1-11; Isaiah 38. The shadow moved back ten steps on the sundial of Ahaz. Hezekiah lived fifteen more years, during which his son Manasseh was born. His healing came from a poultice of figs Isaiah told him to apply to the boil. Hezekiah is also remembered for digging the tunnel that still bears his name, bringing water from the Gihon spring into Jerusalem under siege by the Assyrian Sennacherib.

question: Forty years after fleeing Egypt for killing an Egyptian overseer, Moses was tending his father-in-law Jethro's sheep on the slopes of Mount Horeb. He noticed something strange: a bush that blazed with fire but was not consumed. As he turned aside to look, a voice from the bush called him by name and told him to take off his sandals because the ground was holy. The voice identified itself as the God of his fathers, Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, and commanded him to return to Egypt to free the Israelites. Moses asked for God's name to tell the people. What name did the voice give?
answer: I AM WHO I AM
choices: I AM WHO I AM
I AM ELOHIM
I AM HE
I AM ONE
context: Exodus 3:14. In Hebrew the phrase is 'Ehyeh asher ehyeh.' From the same root comes the four-letter name YHWH (often rendered 'Yahweh' or in English translations as 'the LORD' in small capitals), which the Israelites later regarded as too sacred to pronounce. Moses also got two signs at the bush: his staff turning to a serpent and his hand turning leprous and back again.

question: Moses had been on Mount Sinai forty days receiving the Law from God. The people below, impatient and afraid he was dead, demanded that Aaron make them gods to go before them. Aaron collected their golden earrings, melted them, and cast a golden calf. They sacrificed to it and held a wild feast. As Moses descended carrying two stone tablets inscribed by God himself, he heard the noise of revelry from the camp. When he saw the calf and the dancing, he threw down the tablets and shattered them at the foot of the mountain. What did Moses then do with the golden calf?
answer: Ground it to powder, scattered it on water, and made the people drink it
choices: Ground it to powder, scattered it on water, and made the people drink it
Carried it back up the mountain and buried it under stones
Broke it into pieces and divided them among the twelve tribes
Melted it down and recast it as the lampstand for the tabernacle
context: Exodus 32. About 3,000 men were killed by the Levites that day at Moses's order. Moses then went back up the mountain to plead with God for the people's lives, offering to be blotted out of God's book himself if God would not forgive them. He came back down with a second set of tablets, this time chiseled by Moses but written by God. His face shone so brightly afterward that he had to wear a veil.

question: The shepherd boy David, bringing food to his older brothers at the front, heard the Philistine giant Goliath of Gath taunting Israel's army to send a single champion. Standing nine feet tall in bronze armor weighing 125 pounds, with a spear like a weaver's beam, Goliath had challenged for forty days and no Israelite would face him. King Saul tried to dress David in his own armor; the boy could not move in it and laid it off. David picked five smooth stones from a brook and ran at the giant. A single stone from his sling sank into Goliath's forehead and he fell. The boy had no sword. What did he use to cut off Goliath's head?
answer: Goliath's own sword, drawn from the giant's sheath
choices: Goliath's own sword, drawn from the giant's sheath
His shepherd's bronze hand-axe from his belt
A second smooth stone aimed at the giant's neck
A short hunting blade his brothers had given him
context: 1 Samuel 17. The Philistine army fled when their champion fell. David later kept Goliath's sword as a trophy at the priestly sanctuary of Nob, and famously took it back years later when he was fleeing King Saul (1 Samuel 21:9). David's five smooth stones have entered proverb; some readers note that Goliath had four giant brothers, possibly explaining the spare ammunition.

question: King Darius of Persia, manipulated by his other officials, signed a decree that anyone praying to any god but the king for thirty days would be thrown to the lions. The Hebrew official Daniel kept praying toward Jerusalem three times a day with his window open. The officials reported him at once. Darius spent the night without food, sleep, or music, but had to enforce his own law. At dawn he ran to the sealed den and called out — Daniel answered that an angel had shut the lions' mouths. The king pulled Daniel out unhurt. What did Darius then order done?
answer: Threw the conspiring officials and their families into the same den, where the lions devoured them
choices: Threw the conspiring officials and their families into the same den, where the lions devoured them
Released the lions into the desert and outlawed their hunting from then on
Built a new temple to the Hebrew God beside his own royal palace in Susa
Made Daniel co-regent of all Persia and divided the realm equally between them
context: Daniel 6. Darius then issued a new decree: that all his subjects should reverence the God of Daniel, 'the living God, enduring forever.' Daniel served on into the reign of Cyrus the Great. The story has been read across centuries as a parable of conscience refusing tyrant-worship: 'Daniel kept praying toward Jerusalem three times a day with his window open' is the Hebrew Bible's clearest image of public dissent against compelled assent.

question: Mordecai sent a message to his cousin Queen Esther, urging her to plead with the Persian king Ahasuerus for the lives of the Jews — Haman the vizier had decreed every Jew be killed on a single day. But there was a law: anyone, even the queen, who entered the king's inner court uninvited would be put to death unless the king extended his golden scepter to spare them. Esther had not been called to the king for thirty days. She asked Mordecai for the Jews of Susa to fast with her for three days. Then, dressed in royal robes, she went in. Mordecai's reply to her hesitation has become one of the most-quoted lines in Jewish literature. What did Mordecai say?
answer: Who knows whether you have come to the kingdom for such a time as this?
choices: Who knows whether you have come to the kingdom for such a time as this?
It is better to die a queen than to live a slave in Persia.
The God of our fathers will not abandon his people now.
Even if you fail, the king's mercy is your only shield.
context: Esther 4:14. The king extended his scepter. Esther invited him and Haman to two banquets and, at the second, accused Haman in front of the king. Haman was hanged that same night on the seventy-five-foot gallows he had built for Mordecai. The Jews of Persia were saved, and the festival of Purim still commemorates the rescue with reading the scroll, costumes, and pastries called hamantaschen.

question: A famine had driven the Israelite Naomi and her family from Bethlehem to Moab, where her two sons married local women. When all three men in the family died, Naomi decided to return to Bethlehem. She urged her two Moabite daughters-in-law to stay with their own people. One agreed and went home. The other refused, saying she would follow Naomi anywhere. They arrived in Bethlehem at the start of the barley harvest, destitute. The young widow went into the fields behind the harvesters to glean — that is, to gather leftover grain. The owner of the field, a kinsman of Naomi's, noticed her and ordered his men to leave extra grain on purpose. What was her name?
answer: Ruth
choices: Ruth
Rachel
Rebekah
Hannah
context: The Book of Ruth. Ruth's pledge to Naomi is one of the most beautiful passages in the Hebrew Bible: 'Where you go I will go, and where you lodge I will lodge; your people shall be my people, and your God my God.' Boaz, the kinsman, married Ruth as her redeeming kinsman. Their son Obed was the grandfather of David — making Ruth, a Moabite woman, a great-grandmother of Israel's greatest king.

question: Job was the wealthiest man in the East, with seven sons, three daughters, seven thousand sheep, three thousand camels, and many more flocks. Satan argued before God that Job was only faithful because so blessed; God allowed Satan to test him. In one day four messengers brought ruin: raiders took the oxen and donkeys; fire from heaven consumed the sheep; Chaldeans stole the camels; a great wind collapsed his eldest son's house on all ten of his children at a feast. Job tore his robe, shaved his head, fell to the ground, and worshipped. What did he say?
answer: Naked I came from my mother's womb, and naked shall I return; the LORD gave, and the LORD has taken away
choices: Naked I came from my mother's womb, and naked shall I return; the LORD gave, and the LORD has taken away
Cursed be the day of my birth and the night that announced the conception of a man child
Why have you forsaken me, my God, in this hour of darkness and sudden grief?
Surely the wicked are cast down, and the righteous lift up their heads in the morning
context: Job 1:21. The book of Job is one of the oldest and strangest in the Hebrew Bible — a long meditation on innocent suffering, framed by a prologue and epilogue. Three friends come to comfort Job and end up accusing him; out of the whirlwind God finally answers, not with reasons but with questions: 'Where were you when I laid the foundations of the earth?' Job is finally restored, with new children and double his former wealth.

question: The prophet Elijah challenged the 450 prophets of Baal sponsored by Queen Jezebel to a contest on Mount Carmel. Each side would prepare a bull on an altar but not light the fire — the god who answered by fire was God. The prophets of Baal danced, shouted, and cut themselves with knives from morning until evening; nothing happened. Elijah mocked them: maybe their god was asleep, or on a journey, or relieving himself. Then he rebuilt the altar of God with twelve stones, dug a trench around it, laid the wood and the bull, and poured water over the offering three times until the trench overflowed. Then he prayed once. What happened?
answer: Fire fell from heaven and consumed the offering, the wood, the stones, and the water in the trench
choices: Fire fell from heaven and consumed the offering, the wood, the stones, and the water in the trench
A whirlwind tore the priests of Baal up the slope and out of sight
The bull rose alive from the altar and walked unharmed past the prophets
A bolt of lightning split the altar stones into perfect quarters
context: 1 Kings 18. The people fell on their faces and shouted 'The LORD, he is God! The LORD, he is God!' Elijah then ordered the 450 prophets of Baal seized and killed at the brook Kishon. Jezebel swore she would have Elijah dead by the next day. Elijah fled to the wilderness, sat under a juniper tree, asked to die, and was fed by an angel before walking forty days to Mount Horeb — where God appeared, not in the wind or earthquake or fire but in a still small voice.

question: Gathered with his twelve disciples in an upper room in Jerusalem for the Passover meal on the night before his crucifixion, Jesus announced that one of them would betray him. Each disciple asked, 'Surely not I?' At supper, Jesus said the betrayer was the one he would identify by a specific gesture. He took a piece of bread, dipped it in the dish, and handed it to the one who would betray him. Then he said: What you are going to do, do quickly. Only John, leaning against Jesus, understood. The others thought Judas was being sent to buy something or to give to the poor. Where did Jesus dip the bread before handing it to Judas?
answer: Into the dish of bitter herbs
choices: Into the dish of bitter herbs
Into a cup of red wine
Into a saucer of pure salt
Into a bowl of olive oil
context: John 13:21-30. Judas slipped out into the night; the Gospel notes simply, 'And it was night.' The dipping of the sop into the bitter-herb dish was a sign of special honor at a Jewish meal — Jesus handing it to the man he knew would betray him reads as a final gesture of friendship offered before the break. The Last Supper is the institution of what Christians call the Eucharist or Holy Communion.

question: After the Last Supper, Jesus went with eleven of his disciples to a garden across the Kidron Valley called Gethsemane, on the slope of the Mount of Olives. Knowing what was coming, he asked Peter, James, and John to keep watch with him a stone's throw away, then prayed alone: Father, if you are willing, take this cup from me; yet not my will but yours be done. Luke's Gospel records that he prayed in such anguish that an unusual physical thing happened to him. What did Luke record?
answer: His sweat became like great drops of blood falling to the ground
choices: His sweat became like great drops of blood falling to the ground
His face shone with light so bright the disciples turned away
A wind rose and shook the olive branches with the sound of voices
The earth trembled and split open at his feet for a span of moments
context: Luke 22:39-46. The medical term 'hematidrosis' — sweating blood under extreme stress — is now known to be possible in rare cases. Jesus returned to find Peter, James, and John asleep three times; the third time he woke them with: The hour has come. Get up, let us go. Look, my betrayer is at hand. The garden's name means 'olive press' in Hebrew.

question: While Jesus was still speaking in the garden of Gethsemane, Judas Iscariot arrived with a band of soldiers and temple guards carrying lanterns, torches, and weapons. Judas had given them a signal — the man he kissed would be the one to arrest. He walked up to Jesus and kissed him; Jesus said, Friend, do what you came for. As the soldiers seized him, Peter drew a sword and struck the high priest's servant, slicing off his right ear. Jesus rebuked Peter: All who take the sword will perish by the sword. He then did something for the wounded servant. What did Jesus do, and what was the servant's name?
answer: Healed the man's ear by touching it — the servant was Malchus
choices: Healed the man's ear by touching it — the servant was Malchus
Demanded the soldiers release the man into his care — Demas
Bound the ear in cloth from his own robe — Onesimus
Spoke a blessing over him and continued the conversation — Marcus
context: John 18:10 names the disciple as Peter and the servant as Malchus — the only Gospel to give both names. Luke 22:51 records the healing: 'And he touched his ear and healed him.' It was Jesus's last recorded miracle before his crucifixion. The mention of the right ear is the kind of incidental detail that the early Christians remembered as a marker of eyewitness testimony.

question: After Jesus's arrest in Gethsemane, Peter followed at a distance into the courtyard of the high priest's house, where he sat warming himself by a charcoal fire among the servants. Three times that night people recognized him — a servant girl by the gate, others around the fire, a kinsman of the man Peter had wounded — as one who had been with Jesus. Three times Peter denied it, the last time with cursing and oaths: I do not know the man. At that moment a sound came that Jesus had foretold at the Last Supper. What was the sound, and what did Peter do?
answer: A rooster crowed; Peter went out and wept bitterly
choices: A rooster crowed; Peter went out and wept bitterly
Trumpets sounded from the temple; Peter ran into the night
A horn was blown by the watch; Peter fell to his knees
Dogs began to howl in the courtyard; Peter hid his face in his cloak
context: Matthew 26:69-75; Mark 14:66-72; Luke 22:54-62; John 18:15-27 — the threefold denial is recorded in all four Gospels. Luke adds the detail that Jesus, being led across the courtyard at that moment, turned and looked at Peter. After the Resurrection, by another charcoal fire (John 21), Jesus asks Peter three times 'Do you love me?' — the same Peter who had denied him three times by the first charcoal fire is restored.

question: After his arrest Jesus was taken first to the former high priest Annas for an informal questioning, then bound and led to Annas's son-in-law Caiaphas, the high priest, where the chief priests and the Sanhedrin had assembled. They sought witnesses against him but their testimony did not agree. Finally Caiaphas stood up and put Jesus under oath: I adjure you by the living God, tell us if you are the Christ, the Son of God. Jesus answered. Caiaphas immediately made a specific dramatic gesture, declaring blasphemy. What did Caiaphas do?
answer: Tore his own priestly robes
choices: Tore his own priestly robes
Threw his ring of office on the floor
Covered his face with his hood
Smashed his ceremonial wine cup against the wall
context: Matthew 26:57-66. Tearing the robes was the formal Jewish gesture of mourning or condemnation in response to perceived blasphemy. The Sanhedrin then declared Jesus deserved death — but they had no authority to execute under Roman occupation. They handed him over to the Roman governor Pontius Pilate the next morning. Caiaphas's name is preserved in the ossuary discovered in Jerusalem in 1990.

question: The Roman governor Pontius Pilate, sent up from his coastal capital at Caesarea for Passover security, was handed a prisoner accused of claiming to be a king. He questioned Jesus and concluded: I find no fault in this man. He tried to release him: it was Pilate's custom to release one prisoner of the crowd's choosing at Passover. The crowd chose the bandit Barabbas instead. When Pilate saw he was getting nowhere and a riot was starting, he performed a specific gesture in front of the crowd to declare himself innocent of Jesus's blood. What did Pilate do?
answer: Washed his hands publicly with a basin of water
choices: Washed his hands publicly with a basin of water
Tore the indictment scroll in two and threw it down
Removed his governor's ring and placed it on a tray
Knelt and offered a libation of wine to the temple
context: Matthew 27:24. Pilate said: 'I am innocent of this man's blood; see to it yourselves.' His name was preserved in history by his place in the Gospels and was confirmed archaeologically in 1961 by an inscription at Caesarea Maritima naming Pontius Pilate, Prefect of Judaea. The phrase 'wash my hands of it' for refusing responsibility comes from his gesture.

question: After his trial before Pilate, Jesus was scourged by Roman soldiers, mocked with a crown of thorns and a purple robe, and led out to be crucified. Carrying the crossbeam through the streets of Jerusalem on the way to the hill called Golgotha, he stumbled under its weight. The Roman soldiers pulled a man out of the crowd at random — a man who happened to be passing through, coming in from the country — and forced him to carry the cross the rest of the way. Mark's Gospel names this man, and even names his two sons, suggesting they were known to Mark's first readers. Where was the man from?
answer: Cyrene, in North Africa — his name was Simon
choices: Cyrene, in North Africa — his name was Simon
Antioch, in Syria — his name was Andronicus
Damascus, in Aram — his name was Demas
Ephesus, in Asia — his name was Onesimus
context: Mark 15:21: 'They compelled a passerby, Simon of Cyrene, who was coming in from the country, the father of Alexander and Rufus, to carry his cross.' Cyrene was a Greek colony on the Libyan coast with a large Jewish population. Paul greets a 'Rufus, chosen in the Lord, and his mother' in Romans 16:13 — possibly the same Rufus. Simon's story is the only intersection between Africa and the passion narrative.

question: Two criminals were crucified beside Jesus at Golgotha, one on his right and one on his left. One of them joined in the crowd's mockery: Aren't you the Christ? Save yourself and us! The other rebuked him: We are punished justly, for we are getting what our deeds deserve. But this man has done nothing wrong. Then the second one turned to Jesus and asked one specific thing. Jesus answered him with one of the most-quoted lines from the cross. What did the criminal ask, and what did Jesus reply?
answer: Remember me when you come into your kingdom — Today you will be with me in paradise
choices: Remember me when you come into your kingdom — Today you will be with me in paradise
Save me as well, master — Believe and you shall be made whole
Forgive me, my Lord — Go in peace, your sins are forgiven
Speak my name in heaven — You shall sit at my right hand forever
context: Luke 23:39-43. Christian tradition has given the repentant thief the name Dismas (the unrepentant one is sometimes called Gestas), though the Gospels do not name them. The exchange is the only conversation recorded between Jesus and another crucified person, and the line about paradise is one of the seven traditional 'last words' from the cross.

question: Stephen, one of the seven men appointed by the apostles to administer food to the Greek-speaking Christian widows in Jerusalem, performed wonders and signs among the people. Members of a synagogue argued with him but could not stand up to his wisdom. They brought false witnesses against him and dragged him before the Sanhedrin on charges of speaking against the temple and the Law. Asked to defend himself, Stephen gave a long speech reviewing Israel's history from Abraham forward. He concluded by accusing his accusers in specific words that infuriated the crowd. What did Stephen accuse them of?
answer: Being stiff-necked like their fathers, who killed the prophets and now had betrayed and murdered the Righteous One
choices: Being stiff-necked like their fathers, who killed the prophets and now had betrayed and murdered the Righteous One
Worshipping the Roman emperor in their hearts while pretending devotion to God
Plotting in secret with Pilate to silence the apostles by violence
Breaking the Law of Moses by selling temple offerings to foreigners
context: Acts 7. The crowd covered their ears, dragged him outside the city, and stoned him. As he died Stephen prayed 'Lord Jesus, receive my spirit' and 'Lord, do not hold this sin against them' — echoing Christ's own words from the cross. A young Pharisee named Saul of Tarsus stood watching, holding the cloaks of those who threw the stones, approving the killing. That same Saul would later be struck down on the road to Damascus.

question: Saul of Tarsus, a Pharisee who had approved Stephen's stoning, was traveling to Damascus with letters of authority to arrest any followers of Jesus he found there. Near the city a light from heaven flashed around him; he fell to the ground and heard a voice: Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me? He asked who was speaking. The voice answered: I am Jesus, whom you are persecuting. Saul rose blind, was led by the hand into Damascus, and waited three days without food or drink. A disciple named Ananias was sent — afraid, because he had heard of Saul. Ananias laid his hands on him. What happened?
answer: Something like scales fell from Saul's eyes, and he could see again
choices: Something like scales fell from Saul's eyes, and he could see again
A great wind passed through the room, and Saul fell to his knees
The walls of the house glowed with light, and Saul wept aloud
A bird flew in through the open window and rested on Saul's shoulder
context: Acts 9:18. Saul was baptized at once and began preaching in the Damascus synagogues that Jesus was the Son of God. The local Jews plotted to kill him; his new friends lowered him over the city wall in a basket at night. He took the Greek form of his name, Paul, and became the most influential missionary of the early church, writing letters that make up roughly a quarter of the New Testament.

question: Magi — wise men, probably astrologer-priests from Persia or Arabia — arrived in Jerusalem from the east, asking: Where is the one who has been born king of the Jews? We saw his star at its rising and have come to worship him. King Herod was disturbed, consulted the chief priests about where the messiah was to be born, and learned the answer was Bethlehem. He sent the magi on with instructions to return and report. The star reappeared and led them to the place where the child was. They presented three specific gifts. What were the three?
answer: Gold, frankincense, and myrrh
choices: Gold, frankincense, and myrrh
Spices, silk, and a silver cup
Cedarwood, lapis lazuli, and pearls
Bronze, ivory, and a scroll sealed with wax
context: Matthew 2:1-12. The Gospel does not say there were three magi — only that there were three gifts. Tradition later named them Caspar, Melchior, and Balthasar. Warned in a dream not to return to Herod, they went home by another route. The three gifts have been read symbolically across Christian centuries: gold for a king, frankincense for a priest, myrrh (used in embalming) for one who would die.

question: When King Herod the Great realized the magi had returned to their country by another route without reporting back to him, he was enraged. The star, the magi's question about a born king, the prophecy from Micah about Bethlehem — all of it threatened his throne. He gave orders to kill every male child in and around Bethlehem under a certain age, calculated from the time the star had appeared. Joseph, warned in a dream, fled with Mary and the infant Jesus to safety. Where did they flee?
answer: Egypt
choices: Egypt
Persia
Ethiopia
Phoenicia
context: Matthew 2:13-18. The killing of the children of Bethlehem is remembered in Christian tradition as the Massacre of the Innocents. The flight into Egypt echoes the figure in Hosea 11:1: 'Out of Egypt I called my son.' The holy family stayed in Egypt until Herod died, then returned to Galilee, settling in Nazareth. Herod the Great is the same king who killed members of his own family on suspicion of conspiracy.

question: Years before Jesus began his public ministry, his older cousin John the Baptist appeared in the wilderness of Judea, preaching repentance and baptizing crowds in the Jordan River. He was an ascetic, deliberately recalling the prophet Elijah in his appearance and habits. The Gospels of Matthew and Mark describe his clothing and his diet in specific detail — the kind of detail that helped his first listeners recognize him as a prophet in the old style. What did John wear and what did he eat?
answer: Camel's hair clothing with a leather belt; locusts and wild honey
choices: Camel's hair clothing with a leather belt; locusts and wild honey
A linen tunic dyed white; barley bread and fresh figs
Sheepskin over plain wool; lentils and dried dates
Goatskin and a coarse cloak; bread and the milk of nomads
context: Matthew 3:4; Mark 1:6. The leather belt echoes the figure in 2 Kings 1:8, where Elijah is described as 'a hairy man with a leather belt around his waist.' Jesus came to John for baptism in the Jordan; John protested he was not worthy, but Jesus insisted. As Jesus came up from the water a dove descended and a voice from heaven said: This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased.

question: Herod Antipas, son of Herod the Great, had imprisoned John the Baptist for publicly condemning his marriage to Herodias — his brother's former wife. Herodias hated John and wanted him dead, but Herod feared the prophet and feared the crowds. At Herod's birthday feast, Herodias's young daughter danced before the assembled guests and pleased Herod so much that he swore an oath in front of everyone: Ask whatever you want, even half my kingdom, and I will give it. The girl ran to her mother. What did her mother tell her to demand?
answer: The head of John the Baptist on a platter
choices: The head of John the Baptist on a platter
The release of every Jewish prisoner in Galilee
A throne beside Herod's own in the palace
The destruction of the temple at Caesarea Philippi
context: Mark 6:14-29; Matthew 14:1-12. The girl is unnamed in the Gospels but is identified by Josephus as Salome. Herod kept his oath out of pride before his guests and sent an executioner. John's disciples came, took the body, and buried it. Hearing of John's death, Jesus withdrew from Galilee by boat to a deserted place — where the crowd followed and he fed the five thousand.

question: Seeing crowds gathering, Jesus went up on a mountainside in Galilee, sat down (the teaching posture), and his disciples came to him. He began the longest collection of his teaching in Matthew's Gospel with nine short blessings, each of the same shape: Blessed are the X, for they shall Y. The opening of the first one became proverbial — Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven. The blessings on the meek and the merciful follow; another blessing addresses a specific group with a striking promise. Which group is promised that they shall see God?
answer: The pure in heart
choices: The pure in heart
The peacemakers
The persecuted
Those who mourn
context: Matthew 5:1-12. The nine Beatitudes open the Sermon on the Mount, the longest sustained teaching block in Matthew. Those who mourn are promised they shall be comforted; the meek shall inherit the earth; those persecuted for righteousness gain the kingdom of heaven. The whole sermon runs through Matthew 5-7 and ends with the parable of the house built on rock.

question: After feeding the five thousand, Jesus sent his disciples ahead in a boat across the Sea of Galilee while he went up the mountainside alone to pray. A strong wind came up and the boat was being battered by waves. In the fourth watch of the night the disciples saw Jesus walking toward them on the water and cried out in terror, thinking he was a ghost. He answered: Take courage. It is I. Don't be afraid. Then Peter spoke up. He asked Jesus to do something specific so Peter could verify it was him. What did Peter ask?
answer: Lord, if it is you, tell me to come to you on the water
choices: Lord, if it is you, tell me to come to you on the water
Lord, if it is you, calm this storm with a word
Lord, if it is you, speak my name as you did at the lake
Lord, if it is you, let me see the marks of fire on your hands
context: Matthew 14:22-33. Jesus said 'Come.' Peter got out of the boat and walked on the water — until he saw the wind and began to sink, crying 'Lord, save me!' Jesus reached out his hand, caught him, and said: 'O you of little faith, why did you doubt?' When they got into the boat the wind died down. The disciples in the boat worshipped him, saying: 'Truly you are the Son of God.'

question: After a day teaching parables from a boat, Jesus told his disciples to cross to the other side of the Sea of Galilee. He fell asleep on a cushion in the stern. A sudden squall — the kind for which the Sea of Galilee is notorious, when wind funnels down through the hills onto the lake — swept down on them, breaking waves into the boat and threatening to swamp it. The disciples, several of them experienced fishermen who knew the sea well, woke him in panic: Teacher, don't you care if we drown? Jesus stood up. What did he say to the wind and waves?
answer: Peace, be still!
choices: Peace, be still!
Cease and rage no more!
Be silent and depart!
Storm, hold your peace!
context: Mark 4:35-41. The wind dropped and there was a great calm. Jesus asked: 'Why are you so afraid? Have you still no faith?' The disciples, terrified now in a different way, asked each other: 'Who then is this, that even the wind and the sea obey him?' The Sea of Galilee is fed by snow-melt from Mount Hermon and notorious for sudden violent storms — sailors on the lake today still know its temper.

question: Word reached Jesus that his close friend Lazarus, brother of Mary and Martha at Bethany, was sick. Jesus stayed where he was for two more days before going. When he arrived, Lazarus had been in the tomb four days. Martha went out to meet him on the road: Lord, if you had been here, my brother would not have died. Jesus told her her brother would rise again. She replied: I know he will rise on the last day. He answered with one of the most-quoted sayings in the Gospel of John, a statement about himself and a question to her. What did he say?
answer: I am the resurrection and the life; whoever believes in me shall live, even though they die
choices: I am the resurrection and the life; whoever believes in me shall live, even though they die
Death has no power over the children of Abraham who walk uprightly in righteousness
Weep no more, daughter of Bethany; the dead shall wake on the morning of the last day
Trust in the Father; even the grave shall not hold those you have loved before me
context: John 11. Jesus then asked Martha if she believed; she did. Mary came out weeping. Jesus wept too — the shortest verse in the Bible: 'Jesus wept' (John 11:35). At the tomb, a cave with a stone across the entrance, he ordered the stone rolled away. Martha protested about the smell after four days. Jesus prayed aloud, then called: 'Lazarus, come out!' Lazarus emerged still wrapped in his grave-cloths. Jesus told the crowd: 'Unbind him, and let him go.'

question: After his conversion on the road to Damascus, Saul of Tarsus spent years in Arabia and Damascus before beginning his missionary journeys. He set out from Antioch with Barnabas on what is now called his First Missionary Journey, around 47 AD, through Cyprus and Asia Minor. On Cyprus they were summoned before the Roman proconsul Sergius Paulus, who wanted to hear the word of God. A sorcerer in the proconsul's court opposed them. Saul stared at the man, called him a son of the devil, and struck him with a temporary blindness. The proconsul believed. From that point in the Acts of the Apostles, Saul is consistently called by a different name. What name?
answer: Paul
choices: Paul
James
Mark
Jude
context: Acts 13:9: 'But Saul, who is also called Paul, filled with the Holy Spirit, looked intently at him.' Saul was his Hebrew name; Paul (Paulus) was his Roman one. Many scholars suggest the switch around the encounter with Sergius Paulus is not coincidence — Paul began his mission to the Gentiles publicly under his Roman name. His letters in the New Testament are all written under the name Paul.

question: Fifty days after the Resurrection, the eleven remaining apostles and Matthias (who had replaced Judas Iscariot) and other followers, about a hundred and twenty in all, were gathered in an upper room in Jerusalem. A sound like a violent wind filled the house. Tongues of flame appeared above each of their heads. They went into the street and began preaching — and the Parthians, Medes, Elamites, Egyptians, Romans, and Arabs in the city each heard the apostles speaking in their own native languages. Peter stood up and addressed the crowd, citing the prophet Joel. How many were baptized that day, traditionally counted as the birthday of the Christian Church?
answer: About three thousand
choices: About three thousand
About five hundred
About twelve thousand
Exactly one hundred and twenty
context: Acts 2. The Jewish festival of Shavuot (Weeks, the Greek 'Pentecost' meaning fiftieth day) brought pilgrims from across the diaspora to Jerusalem, which is why so many languages were spoken. Peter's sermon quoted Joel 2:28: 'In the last days, God says, I will pour out my Spirit on all flesh, and your sons and your daughters shall prophesy.' Pentecost is traditionally remembered as the birthday of the Christian Church.

question: The Hebrew Bible opens with one of the most-quoted sentences in any language: In the beginning God created the heavens and the earth. The earth was without form and void, darkness was over the face of the deep, and the Spirit of God hovered over the waters. The first six days of creation each follow the same pattern — God speaks, the thing is, God sees that it is good, evening and morning, the next day. On day one, the first thing God speaks into being is a single named thing, and what follows is the most-quoted phrase from the entire creation account. What does God say on day one?
answer: Let there be light
choices: Let there be light
Let the heavens divide from the earth
Let the waters part and the dry land appear
Let the day rule the morning
context: Genesis 1:3. The order of creation in Genesis 1: day 1 light; day 2 sky (firmament); day 3 dry land and plants; day 4 sun, moon, stars; day 5 sea creatures and birds; day 6 land animals and humans; day 7 God rests. The Hebrew phrase is 'Yehi or' — three syllables, the most-quoted three syllables in any language. In Latin (Vulgate) the line is 'Fiat lux.' Christians and Jews alike have read it for millennia as the moment of cosmic beginning.

question: The story of the binding of Isaac, called the Akedah in Hebrew, is one of the most-dissected passages in religious literature — three days of silent journey, the father instructed to kill the long-promised son. Abraham was a hundred when Isaac was born. By the time of the test Isaac was a teenager or young man, large enough to carry a heavy load up Mount Moriah. Abraham gave the boy something specific to carry up the mountain, while he himself carried the fire and the knife. Christian readers across centuries have read the detail of what Isaac carried as a foreshadowing of another wooden burden carried up a hill outside Jerusalem. What did Isaac carry?
answer: The wood for the burnt offering
choices: The wood for the burnt offering
The rope and cords to bind the animal
The skin of water and the bag of meal
The brass bowl to catch the blood
context: Genesis 22:6. Isaac asked his father on the way: 'Father, here is the fire and the wood, but where is the lamb for a burnt offering?' Abraham answered: 'God himself will provide the lamb.' At the altar Abraham bound Isaac (the Hebrew word akedah means 'binding'), raised the knife, and was stopped at the last second by the angel. A ram was caught in a thicket by its horns. The shofar — ram's horn — blown on Rosh Hashanah remembers that ram. The detail of Isaac carrying the wood up the mountain has been read across Christian centuries as the figure of Jesus carrying his cross up Golgotha; the parallel is one of the oldest Christian typological readings.

question: After ten plagues and the Passover night when the Egyptian firstborn died, Pharaoh let Israel go. Then he changed his mind and pursued them with six hundred chariots. The Israelites, trapped between the Red Sea and the chariots, panicked. A pillar of cloud — that had led them by day, and as a pillar of fire by night — moved between the two camps, so that the Egyptians could not approach Israel through the night. Moses stretched his staff out over the sea; an east wind drove the waters back; Israel crossed dry-shod between two walls of water. At dawn the Egyptian chariots pursued. The wheels of their chariots began coming off. The Egyptians shouted: Let us flee, for the LORD is fighting for them. What did Moses then do, and what happened to Pharaoh's army?
answer: Stretched his staff out again — the waters returned and drowned every chariot, horseman, and the army that had followed
choices: Stretched his staff out again — the waters returned and drowned every chariot, horseman, and the army that had followed
Called fire from heaven — Pharaoh's army was consumed in a moment on the sand
Sounded a trumpet from a high rock — the army turned in fear and was scattered
Lifted his hands in prayer — a great fog descended and the army was lost in it
context: Exodus 14:26-29. The Song of Moses (Exodus 15) follows: 'Sing to the LORD, for he has triumphed gloriously; horse and rider he has thrown into the sea.' Moses's sister Miriam led the women with tambourines in dance. Pharaoh is not named in Exodus, though tradition has variously identified him with Ramesses II. The Red Sea crossing is celebrated each year at the Jewish Passover seder as the founding moment of Israel as a people.

question: After the people had built the golden calf and Moses had broken the first set of tablets, God ordered Moses to chisel two new stone tablets and come back up Mount Sinai. Moses went up alone, taking nothing with him, and stayed there forty days and forty nights, neither eating nor drinking. God passed by him while he hid in the cleft of a rock — Moses was allowed to see only God's back, not his face, for no one could see God's face and live. When Moses came back down with the second set of tablets, something had happened to his face that frightened the people. They could not bear to look at him. What happened to Moses's face, and what did he do about it?
answer: His face shone with light from speaking with God; he wore a veil over it whenever he came down to the people
choices: His face shone with light from speaking with God; he wore a veil over it whenever he came down to the people
His beard had turned snow white; he covered it with the fold of his garment
His eyes glowed like coals from the fire of God; he bound a cloth over them
His skin became pale as ash; he hid his face in his hood
context: Exodus 34:29-35. The Hebrew word for 'shone' is from the same root as 'horn' — and the Latin Vulgate translated it 'cornutus,' giving rise in medieval art to depictions of Moses with horns (most famously in Michelangelo's statue of Moses for the tomb of Julius II in Rome). Paul in 2 Corinthians 3 contrasts the fading glory on Moses's face with the unfading glory of the new covenant. The forty-day pattern recurs at Jesus's wilderness fast, Elijah's journey to Horeb, and the gap between the Resurrection and Ascension.

question: During the wilderness years, the Levite Korah, with Dathan and Abiram of the tribe of Reuben, gathered two hundred and fifty Israelite leaders against Moses and Aaron. Their complaint: You have gone too far, for all the congregation are holy, every one of them, and the LORD is among them. Why then do you exalt yourselves above the assembly of the LORD? Moses fell on his face. The next morning he ordered Korah and his followers to come with their censers, and Aaron with his, and the LORD would show who was holy. The whole congregation gathered. Moses warned them to move away from the tents of Korah, Dathan, and Abiram. As they did, something terrifying happened. What?
answer: The ground opened beneath the rebels and swallowed them, their households, and their possessions alive into Sheol
choices: The ground opened beneath the rebels and swallowed them, their households, and their possessions alive into Sheol
A great wind blew Korah's followers off the side of the mountain into the wilderness
Lightning struck each man's tent and burned them to ashes in moments
Their censers turned to serpents and bit each man at the throat
context: Numbers 16. The two hundred and fifty who had offered incense were then consumed by fire that came out from the LORD. Their bronze censers were beaten into plates to cover the altar — a reminder for the people. The next day the congregation grumbled against Moses and Aaron, blaming them for the deaths; a plague broke out. Aaron ran with his censer between the dead and the living and the plague was stopped. The story has been read for millennia as a warning against challenging legitimate spiritual authority.

question: The king of Moab, Balak, terrified of the Israelites encamped near his border, sent princes to the prophet Balaam with money to come and curse Israel. After consulting God in dreams, Balaam set out riding his donkey, with two servants. An angel of the LORD stood in the way with drawn sword — invisible to Balaam, visible to the donkey. The donkey turned aside into a field; Balaam beat her. The angel moved to a narrow place between walls; the donkey pressed against the wall, crushing Balaam's foot; he beat her again. The angel stood in a place too narrow to turn; the donkey lay down under him. Balaam beat her a third time. Then the LORD did something unprecedented for the donkey. What?
answer: Opened the donkey's mouth and let her speak in his own language
choices: Opened the donkey's mouth and let her speak in his own language
Turned the donkey white as snow as a sign to Balaam to turn back at once
Made the donkey grow wings and fly Balaam back to his own homeland
Caused the donkey to bear a foal that very moment alone on the road
context: Numbers 22:21-35. The donkey said: What have I done to you, that you have struck me these three times? Balaam, having argued with his donkey, then saw the angel and fell on his face. Sent to curse Israel three times, Balaam each time blessed them instead — the famous oracle: 'How fair are your tents, O Jacob, your encampments, O Israel!' (Numbers 24:5) is still recited in synagogue services. Balaam is one of only two animals to speak in the Hebrew Bible (the other being the serpent in Eden). Balaam was later killed by the Israelites in battle (Numbers 31:8).

question: After King Saul had disobeyed God's commands and the kingdom had been torn from him in principle, the prophet Samuel was sent to Bethlehem to anoint a new king from the sons of Jesse. Samuel was nervous — Saul would kill him if he heard. He took a heifer for sacrifice as cover. At Jesse's house he had seven of Jesse's sons pass before him. Eliab was tall and impressive; Samuel thought, Surely the LORD's anointed is before me. God corrected him with one of the most-quoted sentences in the Hebrew Bible. Then Samuel asked Jesse if these were all his sons. Jesse said the youngest was out keeping the sheep. They sent for him. What did God say to Samuel about Eliab — and who was the youngest?
answer: Do not look on his appearance or on his stature — the LORD looks on the heart — and the youngest was David
choices: Do not look on his appearance or on his stature — the LORD looks on the heart — and the youngest was David
Do not measure a man by his strength — the LORD measures by his courage — and the youngest was Asahel
Do not weigh a man by his words — the LORD weighs by his deeds — and the youngest was Eleazar
Do not judge a man by his clothing — the LORD judges by his blood — and the youngest was Ozem
context: 1 Samuel 16:1-13. When David came in he was ruddy, with beautiful eyes and a handsome appearance. Samuel poured the horn of oil over David's head in front of his brothers, and the Spirit of the LORD rushed upon David from that day forward. Saul was tormented by an evil spirit, and his servants sent for a young harp-player to soothe him — David. So David entered the king's court as a musician years before he killed Goliath. The line about the heart has been quoted ever since as a corrective to all judgment by outward appearance.

question: Twenty years after Solomon became king, the temple in Jerusalem was finally complete — built of Lebanon cedar, lined with gold, with two great cherubim of olive wood covered in gold standing inside the inner sanctuary, their wings touching across the room. The Ark of the Covenant was brought up from the city of David in procession by the Levites. The priests carried the Ark into the Most Holy Place, beneath the wings of the cherubim. As they came out, something happened that drove all the priests out of the building and prevented them from continuing the ceremony. What happened?
answer: A cloud filled the house so thick the priests could not stand to perform their service
choices: A cloud filled the house so thick the priests could not stand to perform their service
Fire fell from heaven and consumed the burnt offerings on the altar in a single instant
The earth shook and the walls of the inner sanctuary trembled until the ceremony stopped
A voice spoke from between the wings of the cherubim and the priests fell to the floor
context: 1 Kings 8:10-11; 2 Chronicles 5:13-14. The Hebrew text says: 'the glory of the LORD had filled the house.' Solomon then prayed the long dedication prayer in the courtyard, kneeling with his hands stretched out toward heaven. At the prayer's end, fire came down from heaven and consumed the burnt offering, and the glory of the LORD filled the house again. The temple stood about four centuries until destroyed by Nebuchadnezzar in 587 BC. The Holy of Holies contained only the Ark; after the Babylonian exile, the Second Temple's Holy of Holies stood empty, since the Ark had been lost.

question: Naaman, commander of the army of the king of Aram (Syria), was a great man with his master — but a leper. A young Israelite girl, captured in a raid and now serving Naaman's wife, told her mistress that the prophet in Samaria could cure him. Naaman came with letters from his king, horses, chariots, ten talents of silver, six thousand pieces of gold, and ten changes of clothes. The prophet Elisha did not even come out — he sent a messenger telling Naaman to do one specific thing. Naaman was furious; he had expected the prophet to call on the LORD and wave his hand over the spot. His own servants reasoned with him: If he had told you a great thing, would you not have done it? So Naaman swallowed his pride and did the small thing. What was he told to do?
answer: Go and wash in the Jordan seven times, and his flesh would be restored
choices: Go and wash in the Jordan seven times, and his flesh would be restored
Fast in sackcloth on Mount Carmel for forty days
Carry a clean ox up the mountain and offer it himself
Sleep three nights in the wilderness without food or fire
context: 2 Kings 5:1-19. Naaman dipped himself seven times in the muddy Jordan and his flesh came back like the flesh of a young boy. He returned to Elisha, declared there was no God in all the earth except the God of Israel, and asked to take two mules' load of Israelite soil home with him so he could worship the LORD on Israelite ground. Elisha refused to take payment. His servant Gehazi ran after Naaman, asked for a gift, and lied to Elisha about it — Elisha cursed him with the leprosy that had left Naaman. Jesus refers to Naaman in his synagogue sermon at Nazareth (Luke 4:27).

question: The prophet Ezekiel, in exile by the river Chebar in Babylon, was set down by the hand of the LORD in the middle of a valley full of human bones — very many and very dry. The LORD walked him around them and asked him a question. Ezekiel hedged: O Lord GOD, you know. The LORD told him to prophesy to the bones, and as he did, there was a noise and the bones came together, bone to bone, and sinews on them, and flesh, and skin — but no breath in them. Then the LORD told him to prophesy to the breath. He did, and the breath came into them and they lived and stood on their feet, a vast army. The LORD then explained the vision concerned the house of Israel in exile. What was the question the LORD asked Ezekiel at the start?
answer: Son of man, can these bones live?
choices: Son of man, can these bones live?
Son of man, do you mourn for the dead of Israel?
Son of man, will you carry their names to the king of Babylon?
Son of man, how many days have these lain forgotten?
context: Ezekiel 37:1-14. The vision has been read by Jews across the millennia as a promise of national restoration — the return from Babylon (in 538 BC under Cyrus the Great), the rebuilding of the Temple under Ezra and Nehemiah, and in modern times as a figure for the State of Israel after the Shoah. Ezekiel is uniformly addressed by God as 'son of man' (ben adam) throughout the book — the same Hebrew phrase Jesus most often uses for himself in the Gospels.

question: When Isaac was forty, his father Abraham, old and well-stricken in years, called his oldest servant and made him swear by the LORD that he would not take a wife for Isaac from the Canaanites, but go to Abraham's own kindred and homeland to fetch one. The servant set out with ten camels and treasures. He came to Mesopotamia, to the city of Nahor. By the well outside the city in the evening, when the women came out to draw water, he prayed for a specific sign by which he could recognize the right girl. Within moments a beautiful young woman came out with a jar on her shoulder, drew water for the servant, and then did the specific thing he had prayed for. What was the sign?
answer: That she would not only give him a drink but offer to water all his ten camels too
choices: That she would not only give him a drink but offer to water all his ten camels too
That she would invite him to her father's house for the night without asking his name
That she would offer him a piece of her own bread from the basket on her arm
That she would speak the name of Abraham before he spoke it himself
context: Genesis 24. Watering ten thirsty camels is no small task — each could drink twenty gallons. The girl was Rebekah, granddaughter of Abraham's brother Nahor. Her family agreed, asking her if she would go. She answered with one word: I will go. Isaac was meditating in a field in the evening when the camels arrived; Rebekah dismounted and veiled herself. Isaac took her into his mother Sarah's tent, and the text says he loved her — the first explicit statement of love between man and wife in the Bible.

question: Fleeing his brother Esau after tricking Isaac out of the firstborn's blessing, Jacob ran north toward his uncle Laban's house in Haran. He came one night to a certain place at sunset and stopped. He took one of the stones lying there, put it under his head, and slept. He dreamed of a ladder — or stairway — set up on the earth with its top reaching to heaven, and angels of God ascending and descending on it. Above it stood the LORD, who repeated the promise made to Abraham and Isaac: This land I will give to you and your descendants. When Jacob woke in the morning he was afraid and said: Surely the LORD is in this place, and I did not know it. He set up the stone as a pillar, poured oil on it, and renamed the place. What did he call it?
answer: Bethel — house of God
choices: Bethel — house of God
Peniel — face of God
Mahanaim — two camps
Mizpah — watchtower
context: Genesis 28:10-22. Jacob made a vow: If God will be with me and keep me on this journey, and will give me bread to eat and clothing to wear, so that I come again to my father's house in peace, then the LORD shall be my God, and this stone, which I have set up as a pillar, shall be God's house. The previous name of the place had been Luz; Bethel became one of Israel's holiest sanctuaries. The image of a ladder between earth and heaven has filled Jewish, Christian, and Western art for three thousand years.

question: Falsely accused by Potiphar's wife, Joseph was thrown into the king's prison. The chief jailer recognized his gifts and put him in charge of the other prisoners. Two of Pharaoh's officials — his chief cupbearer (butler) and his chief baker — were imprisoned for offending the king, and Joseph was assigned to attend them. One morning both looked troubled: each had dreamed in the night. Joseph asked them to tell him their dreams. The cupbearer had dreamed of a vine with three branches that budded, blossomed, and produced ripe grapes; he had pressed them into Pharaoh's cup and given it to him. The baker had dreamed of three baskets of bread on his head; birds were eating the bread out of the top basket. What did Joseph interpret the two dreams to mean?
answer: In three days the cupbearer would be restored to his office; in three days the baker would hang on a tree
choices: In three days the cupbearer would be restored to his office; in three days the baker would hang on a tree
Both men would be released in three days to serve the king together at his coming birthday feast
Both men would be executed in three days at the gate of the palace by Pharaoh's own command
Both men would be sent away in three days to serve the king of Cush across the Red Sea border
context: Genesis 40. It happened exactly as Joseph said. Joseph had asked the cupbearer to remember him to Pharaoh when restored. But the cupbearer forgot for two full years — until Pharaoh himself dreamed of fat and gaunt cows, and none of his wise men could interpret it. Then the cupbearer remembered. Joseph was brought up from the dungeon, shaved, and changed his clothes. He stood before Pharaoh and interpreted the dream — and was made second in all Egypt before the day was out.

question: Israel demanded a king from the prophet Samuel, like the other nations had. God told Samuel they had not rejected him but God himself. He warned them what a king would do — take their sons for soldiers and chariots, their daughters for cooks and bakers, their fields and vineyards for himself, a tenth of all their flocks. The people refused to listen. God then sent a young man searching for his father's lost donkeys to the city where Samuel was. He was from the smallest clan of the smallest tribe. He was a head taller than any of the people around him — tall and handsome. Samuel anointed him in private, then summoned the tribes to Mizpah and cast lots: the lot fell on his tribe, his clan, his family, and finally on him. They had to find him; he had hidden among the baggage. Who was he?
answer: Saul, son of Kish, of the tribe of Benjamin
choices: Saul, son of Kish, of the tribe of Benjamin
Eliab, son of Jesse, of the tribe of Judah
Abner, son of Ner, of the tribe of Issachar
Jonathan, son of Hagith, of the tribe of Naphtali
context: 1 Samuel 8-10. Saul began well — defeating the Ammonites at Jabesh-Gilead — but disobeyed Samuel's commands at Gilgal (offering sacrifice himself) and against the Amalekites (sparing King Agag and the best livestock). Samuel told him the kingdom would be torn from him. Saul reigned about forty years, growing increasingly paranoid about his young harp-player and son-in-law David, finally dying with three of his sons at the battle of Mount Gilboa against the Philistines, falling on his own sword to avoid capture.

question: In the spring of the year, when kings go out to battle, King David sent his army out to besiege Rabbah but stayed home in Jerusalem. From the roof of his palace one evening he saw a beautiful woman bathing — Bathsheba, wife of one of his foreign soldiers, Uriah the Hittite. He sent for her, slept with her, and learned she was pregnant. He recalled Uriah from the front hoping he would sleep with his wife and cover the pregnancy. Uriah refused to enjoy a comfort his comrades did not have, sleeping at the palace gate. David then sent Uriah back to the front carrying his own death-order to Joab: Set Uriah in the front of the hottest battle, and withdraw from him so he is struck down. It was done. David took Bathsheba as a wife. The prophet Nathan came to David with a story about a rich man with many sheep who took the poor man's one pet lamb and killed it for a guest. David was furious — That man deserves to die! Nathan answered him with three words. What were they?
answer: You are the man
choices: You are the man
Hear, O king
Repent in dust
Tear your robe
context: 2 Samuel 11-12. David did repent — Psalm 51 is traditionally his prayer after Nathan's confrontation. The child born of the union died. Bathsheba's later son with David was Solomon, who would inherit the throne. David's affair with Bathsheba and arranged murder of Uriah are one of the most-discussed passages in the Hebrew Bible because of how flatly and unsparingly the narrator condemns the king the same book has otherwise celebrated.

question: David's son Absalom — handsome, vain about his hair (which he cut once a year because it grew so heavy), full of grievance over the unpunished rape of his sister Tamar by their half-brother Amnon — rebelled against his father. He won the hearts of Israel by sitting at the city gate hearing complaints. He had himself proclaimed king at Hebron. David fled Jerusalem barefoot, weeping, with a handful of loyal soldiers and friends. After months of civil war Absalom finally engaged David's general Joab in the forest of Ephraim. David's order to all his commanders had been: For my sake, deal gently with the young man Absalom. The battle went badly for Absalom; his army was routed. Absalom himself, riding a mule under a great terebinth oak, met disaster. What happened to him?
answer: His thick hair caught fast in the branches; his mule kept going; he hung between heaven and earth and was killed there
choices: His thick hair caught fast in the branches; his mule kept going; he hung between heaven and earth and was killed there
He was thrown from his mule onto a stake driven into the ground by Joab's men
He was struck by an arrow from a lone archer who did not know him by sight
He was crushed under the falling branch of a great cedar split by lightning
context: 2 Samuel 18. Joab himself drove three darts into Absalom's heart as he hung in the tree. When David heard the news he covered his face and wept aloud: O my son Absalom, my son, my son Absalom! Would I had died instead of you, O Absalom, my son, my son! Joab rebuked him for mourning his rebellious son in front of soldiers who had risked their lives saving the king. Absalom's hair — the source of his vanity — is the cause of his death; the irony is one of the most pointed in Hebrew Bible narrative.

question: Solomon built the Jerusalem temple over seven years, using cedar of Lebanon supplied by King Hiram of Tyre and dressed stone quarried in silence (no hammer or chisel sound in the temple precincts). The Most Holy Place was a perfect cube, twenty cubits on each side, overlaid entirely in pure gold, containing the Ark of the Covenant beneath two great cherubim with wings touching across the room. Outside, before the porch of the temple, two enormous bronze pillars stood — eighteen cubits high (about twenty-seven feet) with capitals of lily-work five cubits tall. They were not load-bearing; they were free-standing and named, with the names recorded in the Hebrew Bible. What were the two pillars called?
answer: Jachin (on the right) and Boaz (on the left)
choices: Jachin (on the right) and Boaz (on the left)
Mizpah (on the right) and Bethel (on the left)
Cherub (on the right) and Seraph (on the left)
Aaron (on the right) and Eleazar (on the left)
context: 1 Kings 7:21; 2 Chronicles 3:17. The name Jachin means 'he will establish'; Boaz means 'in him is strength.' Together: 'in him he will establish strength.' The pillars were broken in pieces by the Babylonians and the bronze carried off when Nebuchadnezzar destroyed the temple in 587 BC (2 Kings 25:13). The two pillars have inspired temple-imagery in Western architecture and in Masonic ritual for centuries. The Babylonian destruction is remembered every year on the ninth of Av (Tisha b'Av).

question: King Nebuchadnezzar of Babylon set up a golden image sixty cubits high on the plain of Dura and decreed that everyone fall down and worship at the sound of horn, pipe, lyre, trigon, harp, bagpipe, and every kind of music. Three young Hebrew officials — friends of Daniel — refused. They were brought before the king. He gave them another chance: bow at the sound, or be thrown into a furnace heated seven times hotter than usual. Their answer was specific and famous: Our God whom we serve is able to deliver us from the burning fiery furnace, and he will deliver us out of your hand, O king. But even if he does not, we will not serve your gods. They were bound in their clothes and thrown in. The flames killed the soldiers who threw them. Looking in, Nebuchadnezzar saw something that astonished him. What?
answer: Four men walking unbound in the fire, and the fourth was like a son of the gods
choices: Four men walking unbound in the fire, and the fourth was like a son of the gods
The three kneeling at prayer surrounded by a perfect circle of golden light
The flames parted into two pillars, the three standing on dry ground between them
A great eagle hovering above them, its bright wings spread like a roof of feathers
context: Daniel 3. The three men's Hebrew names were Hananiah, Mishael, and Azariah; the Babylonian names by which the story is told are Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego. They walked out unsinged — not a hair of their heads scorched, their clothes not even smelling of smoke. Nebuchadnezzar promoted them and decreed that anyone speaking against their God would be torn limb from limb. The three names became a byword for refusing forced worship; the king's question 'Who is the god that can deliver you out of my hands?' has been answered for nearly twenty-six centuries.

question: After the flood, the descendants of Noah migrated and settled in a plain in the land of Shinar. They had one language and the same words. They said to one another: Come, let us build ourselves a city, and a tower with its top in the heavens, and let us make a name for ourselves, lest we be scattered abroad over the face of the whole earth. They made bricks (where there was no good stone) and used bitumen for mortar. The LORD came down to see the city and the tower. He said: Behold, they are one people, and they have all one language, and this is only the beginning of what they will do. Nothing they propose to do will be impossible for them. Come, let us go down and confuse their language so they cannot understand each other. The Hebrew name for the place is a pun on the verb meaning to confuse. What was the place called?
answer: Babel — and the LORD scattered them from there over the whole earth
choices: Babel — and the LORD scattered them from there over the whole earth
Shinar — and the people fled when their words turned to mist in the air
Mizpah — and the people built a watchtower over their broken city
Pithom — and the people sank back into the marshes of the Tigris
context: Genesis 11:1-9. The Hebrew word for 'confuse' is balal — a pun on Babel. Babel is the Hebrew name for the city of Babylon, in Akkadian Bab-ilim ('gate of the gods'). The Tower of Babel has long been associated with the ziggurats — stepped pyramid temples — of Mesopotamia, particularly Etemenanki, the great ziggurat of Marduk in Babylon (the place itself was destroyed by Alexander the Great). Pentecost in Acts 2 is sometimes read as a reversal of Babel: the apostles speaking and being understood across many languages at once.

question: After Elijah was taken up to heaven in the whirlwind, his protege Elisha began his own ministry. Walking from Jericho up to Bethel, he was met by a group of small boys who came out of the city and jeered at him: Go up, baldhead! Go up, baldhead! (The taunt 'go up' was a mocking reference to Elijah's having been taken up into heaven — the implication being that Elisha should follow him.) Elisha turned around, looked at them, and cursed them in the name of the LORD. Something then came out of the woods beside the road. What came out, and what happened?
