answer: Two she-bears that mauled forty-two of the boys
choices: Two she-bears that mauled forty-two of the boys
A swarm of hornets that drove the boys into the city in panic
A pack of jackals that scattered them but harmed none
A pillar of fire that struck them blind for three days
context: 2 Kings 2:23-25. The episode has shocked readers across the centuries — Augustine, Aquinas, and many medieval commentators wrote about it. Some readers point out the Hebrew n'arim k'tannim is better translated 'young men' than 'small boys' — likely teenagers, perhaps prophets of Baal, mocking the LORD's prophet at a roadside outside the Baal-cult center of Bethel; the encounter was no playground teasing but a hostile confrontation. Elisha continued on to Mount Carmel and then back to Samaria. He served as prophet of Israel for about fifty years.

question: Crucified at Golgotha around the third hour of the day (about 9 AM), Jesus hung between two thieves through six hours of agony. From the sixth hour to the ninth hour (noon to 3 PM) darkness covered the land. About the ninth hour he cried out: Eloi, Eloi, lema sabachthani? — My God, my God, why have you forsaken me? — quoting the opening of Psalm 22. Some standing there thought he was calling Elijah and ran to bring him sour wine on a sponge held up on a reed. After receiving the wine Jesus spoke twice more. In John's Gospel his second-to-last word is one short phrase that in Greek (tetelestai) is a single word; commercially it could mean 'paid in full' on a receipt. What was that word?
answer: It is finished
choices: It is finished
Let it be so
I am ready
Behold the king
context: John 19:30. In Luke's account his last words are 'Father, into your hands I commit my spirit' (from Psalm 31:5). The seven 'last words from the cross' across the four Gospels include 'Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they do' (Luke 23:34), 'Today you will be with me in paradise' (Luke 23:43, to the repentant thief), 'Woman, behold your son' (John 19:26-27, to Mary, indicating John), 'My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?' (Matthew 27:46; Mark 15:34), 'I thirst' (John 19:28), 'It is finished' (John 19:30), and 'Father, into your hands I commit my spirit' (Luke 23:46). At his death the curtain of the temple was torn in two from top to bottom.

question: Early on the first day of the week, while it was still dark, Mary Magdalene came to the tomb of Jesus and saw the stone rolled away. She ran to tell Peter and John, who raced back with her. They found the tomb empty, the linen wrappings lying there, and the cloth that had been around Jesus's head folded separately. They went back to their homes; Mary stayed by the tomb weeping. She bent down and looked in: two angels in white sat where the body had been, one at the head and one at the feet, and asked why she wept. Turning around she saw a man she took to be the gardener. He asked: Woman, why are you weeping? Whom do you seek? She said: Sir, if you have carried him away, tell me where you have laid him, and I will take him away. He spoke one word. She recognized him at once and answered in Aramaic. What did each say?
answer: He spoke her name: Mary. She answered: Rabboni, which means Teacher
choices: He spoke her name: Mary. She answered: Rabboni, which means Teacher
He said: Peace be with you. She answered: My Lord and my God
He said: Be not afraid. She fell at his feet and worshipped him in silence
He spoke from beyond the trees. She answered: I have heard your voice
context: John 20:11-18. Jesus then told her: Do not hold on to me, for I have not yet ascended to the Father. Go to my brothers and say to them, I am ascending to my Father and your Father, to my God and your God. Mary Magdalene became the first witness of the Resurrection and the first to bring the news to the apostles — the 'apostle to the apostles' in early Christian tradition. The detail that she at first mistook Jesus for the gardener is one of the small particulars that gave the Easter morning story its power.

question: On the afternoon of the first Easter Sunday, two followers of Jesus were walking from Jerusalem to a village called Emmaus, about seven miles away, discussing the events of the past three days. A stranger joined them and asked what they were debating. They were astonished he had not heard about the crucifixion of their teacher and the women's claim of angels at the empty tomb. He chided them gently: O foolish ones, and slow of heart to believe all that the prophets have spoken! Beginning with Moses and all the prophets, he interpreted to them in all the scriptures the things concerning himself. As they approached Emmaus the stranger acted as though he would go further. They pressed him to stay for the evening meal. At the table he took bread, blessed it, broke it, and gave it to them. What happened next?
answer: Their eyes were opened, they recognized him, and at once he vanished from their sight
choices: Their eyes were opened, they recognized him, and at once he vanished from their sight
He told them his own name and walked them back to Jerusalem in time to find Peter
A great light filled the room and he was carried up through the roof out of sight
The bread itself glowed and he laid both hands on their heads in solemn blessing
context: Luke 24:13-35. They got up that same hour and walked the seven miles back to Jerusalem to tell the eleven. They said to each other on the way: Did not our hearts burn within us while he talked to us on the road, while he opened to us the Scriptures? One of the two is named Cleopas; the other is unnamed. As they finished telling their story, Jesus himself appeared in the locked upper room and said: Peace be with you. The episode is one of the most-painted in Christian art — the moment of recognition at the breaking of bread.

question: On the evening of the first Easter Sunday, the disciples were locked in a room together for fear of the temple authorities. Jesus came and stood among them, said Peace be with you, and showed them his hands and his side. They rejoiced. But Thomas — called the Twin — had not been with them. When they told him, he refused to believe: Unless I see in his hands the print of the nails, and place my finger in the mark of the nails, and place my hand in his side, I will not believe. Eight days later the disciples were again in the room together, with Thomas this time, and the doors were shut. Jesus came and stood among them again with the same greeting. He turned to Thomas. What did he say to Thomas, and what did Thomas reply?
answer: Put your finger here, and see my hands; reach out your hand and place it in my side — and Thomas answered: My Lord and my God!
choices: Put your finger here, and see my hands; reach out your hand and place it in my side — and Thomas answered: My Lord and my God!
Why do you doubt me, Thomas? — and Thomas answered: Forgive me, master, I knew not what I said
Do not be faithless but believing — and Thomas wept and embraced him
Touch the wounds and tell the world — and Thomas answered: I will go to the ends of the earth
context: John 20:24-29. Jesus then added: Have you believed because you have seen me? Blessed are those who have not seen and yet have believed. Thomas's confession 'My Lord and my God' is the highest Christological confession in the four Gospels — calling Jesus directly God. Tradition has Thomas eventually carrying the Gospel to India, where ancient Christian communities (the Thomas Christians) trace their founding to him; he is said to have been martyred near modern Chennai.

question: After the Resurrection, several disciples — Peter, Thomas, Nathanael, the sons of Zebedee, and two others — went fishing on the Sea of Tiberias one night and caught nothing. At dawn a stranger on the beach called out: Children, do you have any fish? When they said no, he told them: Cast the net on the right side of the boat, and you will find some. They did, and could not haul in the net for the great number of fish (153, the Gospel specifies). John recognized first: It is the Lord! Peter wrapped his outer garment around himself (he had stripped to work) and jumped into the sea. They came ashore and found a charcoal fire with fish already on it, and bread. After breakfast Jesus turned to Peter and asked him a question, three times, with slight variations. What was the question?
answer: Simon son of John, do you love me?
choices: Simon son of John, do you love me?
Simon son of John, will you follow me?
Simon son of John, will you preach my Gospel?
Simon son of John, will you stay with me always?
context: John 21. Each time Peter said yes — Yes Lord, you know that I love you — and each time Jesus answered: Feed my lambs / Tend my sheep / Feed my sheep. The threefold question matches the threefold denial in the high priest's courtyard — and the charcoal fire matches the one Peter had warmed himself by that night. Restoration by symmetry. Jesus then foretold Peter's own martyrdom: When you are old, you will stretch out your hands and another will dress you and carry you where you do not wish to go.

question: On the day of Pentecost (fifty days after the Resurrection), the apostles spilled out into the street speaking the languages of every pilgrim in Jerusalem. The crowd was bewildered: How is it that we each hear them in our own native language? Some sneered that the apostles were drunk on new wine. Peter stood up with the eleven, raised his voice, and addressed the crowd in the first Christian sermon ever preached. He began by pointing out it was only nine in the morning, so they could not be drunk. Then he said the speaking in languages was the fulfillment of what an Old Testament prophet had said. Which prophet did Peter cite?
answer: Joel — 'In the last days, says God, I will pour out my Spirit on all flesh; your sons and daughters shall prophesy'
choices: Joel — 'In the last days, says God, I will pour out my Spirit on all flesh; your sons and daughters shall prophesy'
Isaiah — 'A voice cries: In the wilderness prepare the way of the LORD'
Ezekiel — 'I will give you a new heart, and a new spirit I will put within you'
Daniel — 'In the days of those kings the God of heaven will set up a kingdom'
context: Acts 2:14-36. Peter's sermon then moved from Joel through David's prophecies about the Messiah in the Psalms (Psalm 16 and Psalm 110), arguing that David could not have been speaking of himself because David's tomb was still with them — David was speaking of the Christ whom God raised from the dead. The sermon ended: 'God has made him both Lord and Christ, this Jesus whom you crucified.' The crowd was cut to the heart and asked what to do. Peter said: Repent and be baptized. About three thousand were baptized that day. The traditional birthday of the Christian Church.

question: Stephen, one of the seven men appointed by the apostles to administer food to the Greek-speaking widows, was dragged before the Sanhedrin on charges of blasphemy. He gave a long speech recounting Israel's history from Abraham forward, then accused his accusers of betraying and murdering the Righteous One whose coming the prophets had foretold. The crowd ground their teeth at him in fury. Stephen, full of the Holy Spirit, gazed into heaven and said: I see the heavens opened, and the Son of Man standing at the right hand of God. They covered their ears, rushed at him, dragged him outside the city, and stoned him. As they were stoning him, Stephen prayed two things in close succession. The first was 'Lord Jesus, receive my spirit.' The second prayer, said with a loud voice before he died, echoed the figure of Jesus's prayer from the cross. What did Stephen pray?
answer: Lord, do not hold this sin against them
choices: Lord, do not hold this sin against them
Lord, vindicate your servant before the day of judgment
Lord, may my blood plead before the throne for these men
Lord, gather thy servant to the bosom of Abraham
context: Acts 7:59-60. The prayer echoes the figure of Jesus on the cross: 'Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they do' (Luke 23:34). A young Pharisee named Saul of Tarsus stood watching, holding the cloaks of those throwing stones, approving the killing. That same Saul would later be struck down on the road to Damascus and become the Apostle Paul. Stephen is the church's first martyr, and his feast day (December 26, the day after Christmas) is sometimes called Stephen's Day.

question: Sent under guard from Caesarea to Rome to be tried before the emperor (Paul had appealed to Caesar as a Roman citizen), Paul sailed in late autumn. Off Crete he warned the centurion the voyage would end in loss of cargo, ship, and lives. They sailed anyway and were caught by a violent northeast wind called Euraquilo. For fourteen days the storm drove them; they jettisoned cargo and tackle, lost sight of the sun. Paul reassured everyone aboard an angel had told him no life would be lost. On the fourteenth night they grounded on Malta. All 276 aboard reached shore. The Maltese welcomed the survivors with fires. As Paul gathered a bundle of sticks for the fire, something happened that the Maltese took as proof Paul was a criminal pursued by divine vengeance. What happened?
answer: A viper drove out by the heat fastened on Paul's hand; he shook it into the fire unharmed
choices: A viper drove out by the heat fastened on Paul's hand; he shook it into the fire unharmed
A great wave broke over the fire and put it out, leaving the cold survivors in darkness
A wild pig from the village charged into the fire and scattered the burning embers wide
An eagle dropped a stone from above that struck the wood and broke the fire scattered
context: Acts 27-28. The Maltese watched expecting Paul to swell up or fall dead. When he did neither, they decided he was a god. The local chief Publius hosted them; Paul healed the chief's father (sick with fever and dysentery). They wintered on Malta three months, then sailed for Rome on an Alexandrian grain ship called the Twin Brothers (Castor and Pollux). At Rome, Paul lived under house arrest for two more years, preaching to all who came — ending the book of Acts. Tradition has Paul executed (beheaded as a Roman citizen) under Nero, around AD 64-67.

question: In 155 AD an angry crowd at Smyrna demanded the arrest of the elderly bishop Polycarp during the games. Polycarp was eighty-six years old, a disciple of the apostle John, the last living link to the apostolic generation. Friends urged him to flee; he stayed. Brought into the stadium, he refused the proconsul's repeated offers to swear by Caesar's genius and revile Christ. His reply: Eighty and six years I have served Him, and He never did me wrong. How can I now blaspheme my King who saved me? The proconsul threatened wild beasts. Polycarp answered: Call them. He threatened fire. Polycarp said: You threaten fire that burns an hour and is quenched. You know nothing of the fire of judgment. The fire was built. As he was tied to the stake, witnesses reported a strange phenomenon. What?
answer: The flames bent away in an arch like a sail until a soldier ran him through with a dagger
choices: The flames bent away in an arch like a sail until a soldier ran him through with a dagger
A great hailstorm rolled in from the harbor and put out the fire before any wood could catch
His body lifted from the stake and was carried over the stadium roof by a sudden strong wind
The whole stadium was struck dark by an eclipse of the sun just as the fire was being lit
context: The *Martyrdom of Polycarp* (c. 156 AD), a letter sent by the church at Smyrna, is the earliest detailed account of a Christian martyr's death outside the New Testament. The text says a dove flew out from the wound when the soldier struck him. The witnesses collected his bones — more precious than jewels — and kept them as relics. His tomb at Smyrna (modern Izmir) became a pilgrimage site. February 23 is his feast day; he is one of the Apostolic Fathers, alongside Clement of Rome and Ignatius of Antioch.

question: On December 29, 1170, four knights of King Henry II rode into Canterbury Cathedral at vespers. They had taken Henry's furious outburst — Will no one rid me of this turbulent priest? — as a royal command. They first cornered Archbishop Thomas Becket in the cathedral yard at dinner. Becket walked away from them into the cathedral itself for the evening office. The knights followed, armed. The monks tried to bar the doors; Becket forbade it: A church is not a fortress. The knights confronted him at the north transept. Becket refused to leave with them. They drew their swords. The first blow was struck by a specific named knight — one of the four — slicing off the crown of Becket's skull as he stood. Which knight struck first?
answer: Reginald FitzUrse
choices: Reginald FitzUrse
Hugh de Morville
William de Tracy
Richard le Breton
context: The four knights were Reginald FitzUrse, William de Tracy, Hugh de Morville, and Richard le Breton. Tracy, Morville, and Breton followed FitzUrse's blow with their own. The fatal stroke was Breton's, which scattered Becket's brains on the cathedral floor and broke his own sword on the stone. A clerk named Edward Grim, who had stayed beside Becket through the attack, wrote the eyewitness account from which the names come. Becket was canonized just three years later (1173) and his shrine became one of medieval Europe's greatest pilgrimage destinations — the destination of Chaucer's Canterbury pilgrims. Henry II did public penance, walking barefoot to the cathedral and being whipped by the monks at Becket's tomb in 1174.

question: Joan of Arc was nineteen years old when an English-controlled ecclesiastical court at Rouen condemned her as a heretic on May 30, 1431. She had worn men's armor in battle, claimed visits from Saints Catherine, Margaret, and the archangel Michael, broken the siege of Orléans in nine days, witnessed the crowning of the Dauphin as Charles VII at Reims, and been sold to the English after her capture at Compiègne. Her examination ran seventy sessions over five months. She had briefly recanted under threat of execution, then reaffirmed her visions. Pierre Cauchon, the Bishop of Beauvais, pronounced her relapsed and turned her over to the secular arm for burning. She asked for a cross; an English soldier made one from two sticks and gave it to her. As she was led to the stake in the Old Market Square, she wore a specific garment as a sign — and called out a specific word as the fire took her. What was her final word?
answer: Jesus
choices: Jesus
Marie

context: Eyewitnesses reported Joan called the name of Jesus repeatedly as the flames rose, and that her last audible word was the same name. She wore a long white penitential gown (some accounts say with a tall paper hat marked with her offenses). The executioner burned her body twice more to reduce it to ash and threw the ashes into the Seine specifically so French Catholics could not have relics. She was rehabilitated by another church trial in 1456 and finally canonized in 1920 by Pope Benedict XV. Her feast day is May 30. She had been illiterate; the long trial transcripts preserve her voice clearly because she insisted on dictating her answers as precisely spoken.

question: In the sixth month of Elizabeth's pregnancy (Elizabeth being the elderly mother of John the Baptist), the angel Gabriel was sent to a town in Galilee called Nazareth to a young woman engaged to a man named Joseph of the house of David. The young woman's name was Mary. Gabriel came in and said: Greetings, favored one! The Lord is with you. She was troubled at the saying. He told her not to be afraid — she had found favor with God — and that she would conceive and bear a son and call his name Jesus, who would reign over the house of Jacob forever. Mary asked the practical question. What did she ask, and what was Gabriel's answer?
answer: How will this be, since I am a virgin? — The Holy Spirit will come upon you and the power of the Most High will overshadow you
choices: How will this be, since I am a virgin? — The Holy Spirit will come upon you and the power of the Most High will overshadow you
When will this be, Lord? — Before the next Passover has come and gone
Where will this be, Lord? — In a place that you do not yet know
Why has the Lord chosen me? — Because the Lord has remembered the prayers of your fathers
context: Luke 1:26-38. Gabriel added that Mary's cousin Elizabeth, called barren, was already six months pregnant. For nothing will be impossible with God. Mary's reply has been called the model of consent in Western religious thought: Behold, I am the servant of the Lord; let it be to me according to your word. The Latin translation Fiat mihi secundum verbum tuum ('Let it be to me according to thy word') has anchored centuries of Marian devotion and art — the Annunciation is one of the single most-painted scenes in Western art (Fra Angelico, Botticelli, Leonardo, El Greco all painted it).

question: After the angel Gabriel left her, Mary set out with haste into the hill country of Judea to visit her older cousin Elizabeth, who was six months pregnant despite her age. As soon as Elizabeth heard Mary's greeting, the child in Elizabeth's womb leaped for joy, and Elizabeth, filled with the Holy Spirit, cried out in a loud voice: Blessed are you among women, and blessed is the fruit of your womb! Mary then broke into a song of praise that has been sung daily in Christian liturgies for nearly two thousand years — the longest speech given to any woman in the New Testament. It opens with the Latin phrase by which it is best known: Magnificat anima mea Dominum. What is the standard English opening of Mary's song?
answer: My soul magnifies the Lord, and my spirit rejoices in God my Savior
choices: My soul magnifies the Lord, and my spirit rejoices in God my Savior
Blessed be the Lord, the God of Israel, who has visited his people
Lord, now let your servant depart in peace, according to your word
Holy, holy, holy is the Lord of hosts; the whole earth is full of his glory
context: Luke 1:46-55. The Magnificat is a song of social reversal: He has scattered the proud in the thoughts of their hearts; he has brought down the mighty from their thrones and exalted those of humble estate; he has filled the hungry with good things, and the rich he has sent away empty. Echoes of Hannah's song from 1 Samuel 2 run through it. The Magnificat is sung in Christian evening prayer across denominations — at Anglican Evensong, in Catholic Vespers, in Orthodox services. Composers from Bach to Vivaldi to Rachmaninoff have set it.

question: Caesar Augustus had issued a decree for a census of the whole Roman world. Joseph, of the house of David, traveled with his pregnant fiancée Mary from Nazareth in Galilee to his ancestral town of Bethlehem in Judea. While they were there she gave birth to her firstborn son, wrapped him in swaddling cloths, and laid him in a manger — because there was no place for them in the inn. That night in the fields outside Bethlehem, shepherds were keeping watch over their flock by night. An angel appeared and the glory of the LORD shone around them; the angel announced good news of great joy for all people: Born this day in the city of David is a Savior, Christ the Lord. Suddenly there was with the angel a great multitude of the heavenly host. What did they say?
answer: Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to those with whom he is pleased

Praise the LORD, all you nations; extol him, all you peoples!
context: Luke 2:1-14. The Latin Gloria in excelsis Deo ('Glory to God in the highest') has been sung in Christian liturgy for over fifteen hundred years, expanded into the longer Gloria of the Mass. The shepherds went into Bethlehem, found Mary and Joseph and the child in the manger, and went back glorifying God. Luke notes: But Mary kept all these things, pondering them in her heart. The detail of the manger — a feed trough — has shaped every nativity scene in the Western tradition since St Francis built the first one at Greccio in 1223.

question: After thirty years of obscurity in Nazareth as a carpenter, Jesus came to the Jordan River where his cousin John the Baptist was preaching repentance and baptizing crowds. John protested he was not worthy to baptize Jesus — Jesus should baptize him instead. Jesus insisted: Let it be so now; for thus it is fitting for us to fulfill all righteousness. John gave in. As Jesus came up from the water, two specific things happened that the four Gospels all record — a visible sign and an audible voice. What were they?
answer: The heavens opened and the Spirit descended on him like a dove; a voice from heaven said: This is my beloved Son, with whom I am well pleased
choices: The heavens opened and the Spirit descended on him like a dove; a voice from heaven said: This is my beloved Son, with whom I am well pleased

Fire rested on the water around him; a voice from the fire said: I have anointed my king on Zion
context: Matthew 3:13-17; Mark 1:9-11; Luke 3:21-22; John 1:32-34. Immediately after his baptism, the Spirit drove Jesus into the wilderness for forty days, where he fasted and was tempted by Satan three times — to turn stones into bread, to throw himself from the temple pinnacle, to receive all the kingdoms of the world in exchange for worship. The baptism is the start of Jesus's public ministry. The dove has been a Christian symbol of the Holy Spirit ever since.

question: About a week after foretelling his coming death for the first time, Jesus took Peter, James, and John up a high mountain by themselves to pray. As he prayed, his face shone like the sun, his clothes became dazzling white — whiter than any launderer on earth could bleach them, Mark writes. Two figures appeared with him and talked with him about his coming departure. Peter, terrified and not knowing what to say, blurted: Lord, it is good for us to be here; let us make three tents — one for you, one for Moses, and one for Elijah. As he was still speaking, a bright cloud overshadowed them and a voice spoke from the cloud, the same voice that had spoken at Jesus's baptism. Who were the two figures with Jesus, and what did the voice say?
answer: Moses (the Law) and Elijah (the Prophets) — and the voice said: This is my beloved Son, with whom I am well pleased; listen to him
choices: Moses (the Law) and Elijah (the Prophets) — and the voice said: This is my beloved Son, with whom I am well pleased; listen to him

context: Matthew 17:1-9; Mark 9:2-10; Luke 9:28-36. The mountain is traditionally identified as Mount Tabor in Galilee, though some scholars favor Mount Hermon. Moses and Elijah together represent the Law and the Prophets — the two great divisions of the Hebrew Bible. Both had had mountain encounters with God (Moses at Sinai, Elijah at Horeb). Both had unusual departures (Moses buried by God, Elijah taken up in a chariot of fire). Jesus told the three disciples not to tell anyone of the vision until after he had risen from the dead.

question: Five days before his crucifixion, Jesus rode into Jerusalem from Bethphage at the foot of the Mount of Olives on a young donkey he had sent two disciples to fetch. The chosen mount echoed the figure in Zechariah 9:9: Rejoice greatly, O daughter of Zion! Behold, your king comes to you, humble and riding on a donkey. The crowds, who had heard he had raised Lazarus from the dead a few days earlier in Bethany, ran out from Jerusalem to meet him. They spread their cloaks on the road. They cut palm branches from the trees and waved them as he passed. What did the crowds shout?
answer: Hosanna! Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord! Hosanna in the highest!
choices: Hosanna! Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord! Hosanna in the highest!
Alleluia! The kingdom has come, the kingdom of David! Alleluia in the highest!

context: Matthew 21:1-11; Mark 11:1-11; Luke 19:28-44; John 12:12-19. 'Hosanna' is Hebrew/Aramaic for 'save now' — the prayer in Psalm 118:25-26 from which the cry comes. The Pharisees told Jesus to rebuke the crowd. He answered: I tell you, if these were silent, the very stones would cry out. The episode is celebrated each year on Palm Sunday at the start of Christian Holy Week. Within five days the same Jerusalem crowd would be shouting Crucify him! The reversal is one of the most-discussed contrasts in the Gospels.

question: After his baptism by John the Jordan, Jesus was driven by the Spirit into the wilderness, where he fasted forty days and forty nights. At the end he was hungry. The devil came to him. The first temptation was the most direct one to a starving man: If you are the Son of God, command these stones to become loaves of bread. Jesus answered with a quotation from Deuteronomy 8:3. The devil then took him to the pinnacle of the temple, told him to throw himself down (citing Psalm 91 that angels would catch him); Jesus quoted Deuteronomy 6:16 in reply: Do not put the Lord your God to the test. Finally the devil took him to a very high mountain, showed him all the kingdoms of the world, and offered them in exchange for worship; Jesus quoted Deuteronomy 6:13 in reply and drove him off. What was Jesus's answer to the first temptation?
answer: Man does not live by bread alone, but by every word that comes from the mouth of God
choices: Man does not live by bread alone, but by every word that comes from the mouth of God

context: Matthew 4:1-11; Luke 4:1-13; Mark 1:12-13. Each of the three Jesus-replies is from Deuteronomy. After the devil left, the Gospel says, angels came and ministered to him. The temptations have been read across centuries as the three pulls of all human ambition — appetite (turn stones to bread), spectacle (throw yourself down from the temple roof), and power (worship me and the kingdoms are yours). Dostoevsky's Grand Inquisitor in *The Brothers Karamazov* devotes a famous chapter to expounding what the three temptations meant.

question: Paul, waiting in Athens for Silas and Timothy to catch up, was provoked by the abundance of idols in the city. He argued daily in the marketplace with anyone he met. Some Epicurean and Stoic philosophers brought him to the Areopagus — the hill of Ares, the Greek court where philosophical and religious questions were debated. They said: May we know what this new teaching is that you are presenting? Paul stood in the middle of the Areopagus and began: Men of Athens, I perceive that in every way you are very religious. For as I passed along and observed the objects of your worship, I found also an altar with a specific inscription. What I now proclaim to you, you already worship as unknown. What was the inscription on that altar?
answer: To an unknown god
choices: To an unknown god

context: Acts 17:16-34. Paul went on to quote a Greek poet — In him we live and move and have our being (likely Epimenides) — and another — For we are indeed his offspring (Aratus, *Phaenomena*). When he mentioned the resurrection of the dead, some mocked him, others said: We will hear you again about this. A few believed, including Dionysius the Areopagite (a member of the court) and a woman named Damaris. The Areopagus sermon has been studied for centuries as a model of cross-cultural argument — meeting the audience inside their own framework before pushing past it.

question: After the Resurrection Jesus appeared to his disciples over forty days, eating with them, opening the scriptures to them, and instructing them. Then he led them out as far as Bethany, raised his hands, and blessed them. As he blessed them he was carried up into heaven; a cloud took him out of their sight. As they were gazing into the sky, two men in white stood beside them and said: Men of Galilee, why do you stand looking into heaven? This same Jesus, who was taken up from you into heaven, will come in the same way. Before his ascension Jesus had given a specific final commission in Matthew's Gospel, summarizing what the disciples were to do until he returned. What was that final commission?
answer: Go and make disciples of all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit

The Acts version specifies the disciples will be Jesus's witnesses in Jerusalem, in all Judea and Samaria, and to the end of the earth. The Mount of Olives (and Bethany on its eastern slope) is the traditional site of the Ascension; the Chapel of the Ascension still stands there. The Ascension is celebrated forty days after Easter in the Christian calendar.
